at_rest.encrypted: The volume holding the data is encrypted ({{layer}}). The instance cannot know how it is unlocked at start-up, though: whoever administers it declares that part.
at_rest.no_block_devices: This system does not expose information about its block devices: whether the data is encrypted cannot be verified.
at_rest.no_mount_table: This system does not expose its mount table: the instance cannot tell whether the data volume is encrypted.
at_rest.none: No encryption found on the data volume ({{filesystem}}). If the disk is encrypted by its firmware or hardware, the instance cannot see it: the protection to check is the NAS's own.
at_rest.none_but_automatic: No encryption found on the data volume ({{filesystem}}). If the disk is encrypted by its firmware or hardware, the instance cannot see it: the protection to check is the NAS's own. But the configuration declares encryption with automatic unlocking: one of the two is wrong, and until you sort it out, consider the data NOT protected.
at_rest.none_but_passphrase: No encryption found on the data volume ({{filesystem}}). If the disk is encrypted by its firmware or hardware, the instance cannot see it: the protection to check is the NAS's own. But the configuration declares encryption with a passphrase at start-up: one of the two is wrong, and until you sort it out, consider the data NOT protected.
at_rest.volume_not_found: I could not find which volume holds {{path}}: whether it is encrypted cannot be verified.
at_rest.zfs: The data is on ZFS, where encryption is a property of the dataset that cannot be read from the block devices. Check it with `zfs get encryption`.
backup.healthy_days_one: Last one {{count}} day ago. One every {{interval}} hours, keeping the last {{keep}}.
backup.healthy_days_other: Last one {{count}} days ago. One every {{interval}} hours, keeping the last {{keep}}.
backup.healthy_hours_one: Last one {{count}} hour ago. One every {{interval}} hours, keeping the last {{keep}}.
backup.healthy_hours_other: Last one {{count}} hours ago. One every {{interval}} hours, keeping the last {{keep}}.
backup.healthy_recent: Last one less than an hour ago. One every {{interval}} hours, keeping the last {{keep}}.
backup.memory_warning: This instance holds {{stored}} and the container has a memory limit of {{limit}}. A backup needs about {{needed}}, because the archive is encrypted entirely in memory: below that, the system kills the process without writing anything to the logs, and the instance restarts. Raise the container's memory limit, or move the backups off the instance.
backup.missing: On in principle, but there is no archive. They are not working: check the logs for “backup_failed”.
backup.not_configured: Not on yet. You can set them up below in a minute.
backup.stale_days_one: The last one is from {{count}} day ago, but they should come every {{interval}} hours. Something has stopped: check the logs for “backup_failed”.
backup.stale_days_other: The last one is from {{count}} days ago, but they should come every {{interval}} hours. Something has stopped: check the logs for “backup_failed”.
backup.stale_hours_one: The last one is from {{count}} hour ago, but they should come every {{interval}} hours. Something has stopped: check the logs for “backup_failed”.
backup.stale_hours_other: The last one is from {{count}} hours ago, but they should come every {{interval}} hours. Something has stopped: check the logs for “backup_failed”.
backup.stale_recent: The last one is from less than an hour ago, but they should come every {{interval}} hours. Something has stopped: check the logs for “backup_failed”.
backup.waiting: On. The first archive arrives within a minute of start-up.
connection.local: You are on the same network as the instance: nobody else is in between.
connection.loopback: You are looking at the instance from the machine that hosts it.
connection.overlay: You are coming from outside home, through the pilot's private network. Content stays encrypted all the way to the instance, but whoever runs that network sees that you connected, when and from where.
connection.public: You are coming from an address that belongs neither to the home network nor to the pilot's private network. It may mean the instance can be reached from the Internet, or that there is a proxy between you and it: whoever administers it should check which.
durability.anonymous: The data is on an **anonymous** Docker volume (`{{volume}}`), mounted on {{mountPoint}}: nobody asked for it, so nobody carries it over. **It survives only if you update with `docker compose`**; if you recreate the container from the NAS panel, from Portainer, with Watchtower or by hand, Docker attaches a new, empty one and the instance starts from scratch — accounts, content, photographs and the private key, which cannot be replaced. Mount a folder of yours or a named volume on {{mountPoint}}.
durability.ephemeral: The data is inside the container, in {{path}}, and not on a volume. **It will disappear at the next image update**: accounts, content, photographs and the instance's private key, which cannot be replaced. Stop the instance and mount a folder or a volume on {{path}} before using it for real.
durability.host: The data is in {{path}}, on a filesystem of this machine.
durability.no_mount_table: This system does not expose its mount table: the instance cannot tell whether its data will survive an update.
durability.persistent: The data is on a volume mounted on {{mountPoint}}, so it survives image updates.
durability.volume_not_found: I could not find which volume holds {{path}}: whether the data will last cannot be verified.
ping.refused: The other instance refused the request.
ping.via_relay: Reached through a relay: the direct connection did not get through.
probe.echo_mismatch: The other instance answered something different from what it was sent.
probe.not_active: The network probe is not on for this instance: switch it on with ESTIA_NETWORK_PROBE.
probe.off: The network probe is off, which is the default: switching it on makes this instance reachable by another instance that knows its public key, and that is not something an update should decide for whoever administers it. It measures whether two instances really find each other (ADR 0018); it carries no content.
probe.ready_internet: This instance can be reached **by its public key alone**: that is the only thing to give another instance, and it does not expire. To be found it uses iroh's public servers, which see who looks for whom but carry no content: no content passes through here at all.
probe.ready_local: This instance can be reached by public key on the local network, with no third-party infrastructure. There is no discovery here, so the key alone is not enough: the other instance needs the code below, which also carries the addresses.
probe.unavailable: The network probe is on, but its component is not available on this machine: {{reason}}. Everything else on the instance works normally.
probe.unavailable_no_reason: The network probe is on, but its component is not available on this machine: no reason was given. Everything else on the instance works normally.
probe.via_relay: Reached, but through a relay: the direct connection did not work.
reach.direct: Reached over a direct connection, with nobody in between.
reach.key_needs_internet: Not reached: This is a public key, but the network is set to “local”, where there is no discovery: nobody can tell where that key lives. Switch to “internet”, or use the other instance's long code, which also carries its addresses.
reach.network_off: Not reached: The network between instances is not on for this instance.
reach.not_a_key: Not reached: This is neither a public key nor another instance's code. The key is the short line the other instance shows in its own panel.
update.available: There is a new version: you are on {{current}}, the registry has {{latest}}. You update from the machine's terminal, with the commands below.
update.command.cli.note: It is the one command if you have the CLI installed: it downloads the new image, detects whether you use Compose or a single container, and recreates the instance keeping its port and data volume.
update.command.cli.title: With the “estia” command (recommended)
update.command.compose.note: The CONFIG FILES column says where this instance's file is. Then, in that folder: `cd THE_FOLDER && docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`.
update.command.compose.note_container: It finds the folder by itself: this instance knows its own container id ({{id}}), and Docker knows where it created it. If it was not Compose that created it, it does not even try: it tells you so and stops.
update.command.compose.title: Or by hand — step 2: if Compose created the instance — recreate it from its folder
update.command.install_script.note: It is the same command you install with: it downloads the new image and remakes the container, so the data stays where it is. It stops by itself, touching nothing, if it finds a container that keeps its data elsewhere.
update.command.install_script.note_volum: It is the same command you install with: it downloads the new image and remakes the container on the same “{{volume}}” volume, so the data stays where it is. It stops by itself, touching nothing, if it finds a container that keeps its data elsewhere.
update.command.install_script.title: Or by hand — step 2: if you installed it with the single command — run it again
update.command.pull.note: This only downloads: on its own it updates nothing, and the container keeps running the old image until you recreate it — the command below does that. And it does not depend on the folder you are in: `docker pull` talks to Docker, not to the files you have there.
update.command.pull.title: Or by hand — step 1: download the image
update.command.recreate.note: This recreates nothing: it **prints** the command that remakes this container exactly as it is — name, ports and folders taken from Docker rather than from your memory. Read the line: after each `-v` there must be the place where your data really is. Then `docker rm -f {{id}}` and paste the printed line.
update.command.recreate.title: Or by hand — step 2: if the NAS panel or `docker run` created it — remake it as it is
update.command.save_data.note: This instance's data is inside the container: recreating it to update it deletes the data — accounts, content, photographs and the private key, which cannot be replaced. Copy it out, mount a named volume, and only then update. The steps are in the installation guide.
update.command.save_data.title: The data first, then the update
update.installation.anonymous: This instance runs in a container, with its data on an anonymous volume.
update.installation.bind: This instance runs in a container, with its data in a folder of the machine.
update.installation.ephemeral: This instance runs in a container and keeps its data inside itself.
update.installation.volume: This instance runs in a container, with its data on the “{{volume}}” volume.
update.installation.volume_unnamed: This instance runs in a container, with its data on an unnamed volume.
update.registry_unreachable: I can't reach the registry ({{reason}}). Try again when the machine can reach the Internet.
update.unknown_revision: This installation does not declare which commit it was built from — typical of a test from source, or of an image older than this comparison. I can't tell whether you are behind: updating anyway is the shortest way, and afterwards the image will declare it, so next time it will be known.
update.up_to_date: You are already on {{current}}, the latest published on {{channel}}.
upgrade.backup_created_one: Before applying one migration, the instance wrote an encrypted backup: {{name}}. It is this update's point of return.
upgrade.backup_created_other: Before applying {{count}} migrations, the instance wrote an encrypted backup: {{name}}. It is this update's point of return.
upgrade.backup_failed_one: The backup that should have come before one migration failed ({{reason}}), and the migration was applied anyway so as not to leave the instance stopped. This update has no point of return: the backups you believe you have are not working, and need checking now.
upgrade.backup_failed_other: The backup that should have come before {{count}} migrations failed ({{reason}}), and the migrations were applied anyway so as not to leave the instance stopped. This update has no point of return: the backups you believe you have are not working, and need checking now.
upgrade.no_backup_one: The instance applied one migration without writing a backup, because none is configured. Migrations only go forward: this update has no point of return, and cannot have one later. Set a public key in Settings → Backups so that the next one has it.
upgrade.no_backup_other: The instance applied {{count}} migrations without writing a backup, because none is configured. Migrations only go forward: this update has no point of return, and cannot have one later. Set a public key in Settings → Backups so that the next one has it.
